objectives: Explain what long-term singleness describes, and what it does not describe.
Tell the difference between the state of being single and the story a person tells about it.
Name the words that describe the state, the history and the choice, and use them accurately.
Recognise the social pressure and the stigma that sit under the ordinary stories people tell.
Compare four common situations of a single life and say what usually helps in each one.
Run a five-step routine that keeps a single life steady.
Answer the questions colleagues, relatives and strangers actually ask.

sections.body:
**Long-term singleness** is the state of having no romantic partner over a long stretch of adult life. It describes an arrangement, in the way that 'a long night shift' describes an arrangement. It says what the situation is. It does not say what the situation means to the person living it, and it does not say whether the situation is good.

Three things get confused with it, and this article keeps them apart. Singleness is not a diagnosis: no medical or psychological condition is named by it, and nothing in it needs treating. It is not a failure: a life with a partner is not the only life that counts, and nothing about a single life says the person did something wrong. And it is not the same as being alone. A single person can be with people all day and feel alone at night; a partnered person can live in a house full of people who do not know them.

The distinction that matters most is between the state and the story. The **state** is a set of facts: no partner, a number of years, a certain amount of contact with other people, a certain amount of time alone. The **story** is what the person says about those facts, to themselves and to others. It may be confident, apologetic, proud, tired or evasive. Two people in exactly the same state can tell completely different stories, and the story often changes while the state does not.

Whether a long single life is good for a given person is not settled, and this article does not pretend otherwise. Some accounts put the main costs on the practical side: sharing a rent, splitting the work of an illness, having somebody in the room when something goes wrong. Other accounts put them on the social side: the pressure, the assumptions, being the exception in a room. Both describe real experience, and the balance depends on the person and the place. The useful thing to do is smaller than settling that argument: name the state accurately, tell a story that is true, and keep the machinery of an ordinary life in working order.
examples: Singleness is a state, and it is not a verdict.
I am single; that is a fact about my life at the moment, and not a diagnosis.
Being single and being alone are different things.
The state has been the same for years, and the story about it has changed.
sections.heading: What long-term singleness is, and what it is not

terms.example: She has been a single for years, and she describes it as a period of her life, not as a problem.
terms.gloss: The state of having no romantic partner, and the person in that state.

terms.example: Long-term singleness has its own vocabulary, and its own pressures.
terms.gloss: The situation of being without a romantic partner, seen as a general condition rather than one person's story.

terms.example: He said he was unpartnered, and he said it without any apology in his voice.
terms.gloss: Describing a person who has no romantic partner, without saying whether that is a choice.

sections.body:
The single years are not a gap between the other parts of a life. They are years with their own content, and the content is mostly ordinary: a job, a commute, a class, a phone call to a sister, and a series of small decisions about what to do with an evening.

**Friendship** does more work in a single life than in a partnered one, because there is less else for it to do. People lean on a small number of close relationships for practical business as well as for company: a lift to the airport, a second opinion, somebody to tell when the news is bad. This is not a lesser version of a relationship. It is a different set of skills — keeping a friendship alive over years without the daily contact a shared household provides, and asking for something without the awkwardness of being owed it.

**Solitude** and loneliness are not the same thing, and the difference is worth keeping. Solitude is the state of being alone. Loneliness is the state of feeling that the connection you want is not there. One person can have a full week of company and feel lonely on a quiet Sunday evening; another can live alone for years and not feel lonely at all. The two often travel together, which is exactly why one of them is not a reliable sign of the other.

The parts that are genuinely harder should be said plainly, because an article that lists only the good parts teaches nothing. Some things cost more when you are single: sharing a rent, dividing the work of an illness, somebody to call at midnight after bad news, the practical company of a person who knows your life. Other things are different rather than worse: a holiday is planned by you, a room stays yours, nobody has to negotiate how the evening ends. Which side dominates depends on the person, the place and the stage of life. **The psychology of long-term singleness is mostly the psychology of holding that difference** — between what is easier and what is harder, and between the state and the story about it.
examples: Solitude is the situation; loneliness is the feeling. They are different words.
The years are not empty. They have their own shape.
I have friends, and I call one of them when something goes wrong.
Some things are harder alone, and some things are easier. Both lists are true.
sections.heading: What the single years actually contain

sections.body:
Almost everybody can describe the situation better than they can describe the pressure around it. Three stories come up again and again in conversations about long-term singleness. Each of them is useful. Each of them leaves something out.

The first is the **career story**: 'I am focusing on my work.' It is often true, and it does useful work as an answer, because it ends the conversation politely. The second is the **standards story**: 'I know what I want, and I am not going to settle.' It protects a person's judgement from the question 'why are you still alone?', and it is sometimes the actual reason a relationship ends. The third is the **contentment story**: 'I am happy on my own.' It is the easiest to say and the hardest to defend, because a listener who has doubts has no way to check it.

Underneath all three there is usually a fourth subject that nobody names: **social pressure** — the repeated, low-grade sense that being single is a condition to be explained, corrected or eventually ended. It rarely arrives as one cruel remark. It arrives as a colleague who asks 'any news?' with a raised eyebrow, as a relative who has not given up, as a form that asks for a status you do not have. The pressure is not the same as **stigma**, which is stronger and more visible: a stigma is a mark of disgrace attached to the status itself. Some workplaces and some families carry a real stigma against a long single life; others carry almost none. That difference is cultural, not personal.

The wider question is not settled. Some accounts put the main cost of a long single life in the pressure and the assumptions, and treat the distress as something other people produce. Others put it in the practical side, and treat the pressure as a matter of badly handled conversations. The two accounts do not cancel each other out, and this article does not pick a winner. What both point to is the same work: a story that is true enough to carry the pressure, and a set of habits that hold up when the pressure and the practical difficulties arrive together.
examples: I am focusing on my work this year, and I am happy with that.
I know what I am looking for, and I am not going to rush it.
I am single, and it is not a problem that needs solving.
The pressure is real, and it is not about a relationship I have not found.
sections.heading: The stories people tell about being single

terms.example: The social pressure arrives in small questions, not in one cruel remark.
terms.gloss: The repeated sense that a status such as being single is a condition to be explained, corrected or ended.

terms.example: In some offices there is a stigma against a long single life, and in others there is none.
terms.gloss: A mark of disgrace that a group attaches to a status, so that the status itself becomes hard to show.

terms.example: Her contentment with the arrangement was visible in the way she answered people.
terms.gloss: A settled sense that a situation is acceptable, without the need for it to be improved first.

sections.body:
Singleness has a small and precise vocabulary, and most of the confusion in a conversation comes from using the wrong word. These are the words worth knowing, grouped by what they describe: the state, the history, the choice and the standing. A person is **partnered** when they have a romantic relationship, and **unpartnered** when they do not, whether or not they live with somebody. Two partnered people who live in the same home **cohabit**: they are not married, and the word says nothing about how serious the relationship is.

Three words describe the history that led to the present. A person is **divorced** when a marriage has ended legally. A person is **widowed** when a spouse has died. When the two people end a marriage without the law turning it into a fight, the separation is **amicable**: they divide what has to be divided, they arrange the children, and they stay on speaking terms. Note what *amicable* does not say. It does not say the marriage was good, and it does not say the friendship will last.

Two phrases describe the choice. **Voluntary singleness** is the state of being single because that is where you have put yourself: waiting on purpose, or working on something else, or living without a partner as a decision. **Involuntary singleness** is the state of being single because the wish for a partner has not been met: the meeting has not happened, or the wish has not been strong enough, or the timing has not come. In practice the two mix. A person who says 'single by choice' and a person who says 'single by circumstance' are describing different mixtures, not two fixed kinds of person.

One phrase describes where you stand. **Romantic availability** means the person is open to a relationship and would say yes to the right one. It is a statement about willingness, not about desire, and it is not the same as being single: a person can be single and not available, and the reason is usually worth saying out loud instead of leaving somebody else to guess it.
examples: I am not partnered at the moment, so I will go on my own.
They cohabit; they have not married.
The separation was amicable, so we still speak.
I am not looking for a relationship at the moment, and I am not ruling it out either.
sections.heading: The words of singleness

terms.example: She is partnered, and her partner works in another city.
terms.gloss: Describing a person who has a romantic relationship, whether or not they live with the other person.

terms.example: They have cohabited for three years and still keep two homes.
terms.gloss: To live with a partner in the same home without being married to that person.

terms.example: He is divorced, and the children spend the week with him.
terms.gloss: Describing a person whose marriage has ended legally.

terms.example: She is widowed, and she still keeps the shared photographs on the wall.
terms.gloss: Describing a person whose spouse has died.

terms.example: The separation was amicable, so the flat was sold without a lawyer's fight.
terms.gloss: Describing an ending in which the two people settle the practical matters and stay on speaking terms.

terms.example: He calls it voluntary singleness, and he means it as a decision rather than a consolation.
terms.gloss: Being single because that is the arrangement the person has chosen.

terms.example: She calls it involuntary singleness, and she has stopped apologising for it.
terms.gloss: Being single because the wish for a partner has not been met, rather than by choice.

terms.example: His romantic availability changed when he moved to another city, and he says so openly.
terms.gloss: The state of being open to a relationship and willing to say yes to the right one.

sections.body:
Four situations get mixed together in ordinary conversation, and they need different answers. A person is a **voluntary single** when the single life is the plan. A person is an **involuntary single** when the plan is still to find a partner. A person is single **after a long relationship** when a partnership or marriage has ended recently, and the shape of those years is still with them. A person is single **by circumstance** when something outside the search changed the plan: a move, a visa, an illness, a caring responsibility, a long posting somewhere remote.

The table gives three columns for each situation. The first is what it looks like **from inside**: the private view, which is rarely the view from outside. The second is **what other people assume**, and this is where the social pressure enters. The third is **what usually helps**: the practical step that moves the situation forward.

Read the second column carefully, because that is where the mistakes are made. The assumption is usually taken from a template and then treated as a fact. A person who has been single for years is often assumed to be choosing; a person who says they are choosing is often assumed to be waiting for something better. Neither assumption is what the person said, and both are corrected in one sentence.
examples: I am single by circumstance: I moved here for the work, and I have not met anybody yet.
I am not waiting for the right person. This is how I live.
We separated amicably, and I am still in the same flat.
I am single, and I am open to a relationship if it comes.
sections.heading: Four kinds of single life, and how each one is read

headers: What it looks like from inside
rows: Voluntary single: the single life is the plan.
The days are arranged around work, friends and personal projects, and there is no sense of something missing.
That it is a phase before the real life starts, or a claim to be above the ordinary.
Saying plainly that this is the plan, and naming what it makes possible.
Involuntary single: the wish for a partner is still there and has not been met.
The ordinary days go well; the missing partner shows up in small moments, at night and in plans for two.
That something is wrong with the person, or that the person is not trying.
Widening the ordinary routes to meeting people, and asking for help without treating it as a confession.
Single after a long relationship: the last years still set the rhythm.
The flat, the calendar and the way a day ends are still shaped by somebody who is not there.
That the ending is finished and the person is over it.
Naming what is still in the habits, the housing and the dates, and clearing the practical part first.
Single by circumstance: something outside the search changed the plan.
The relationship was not the problem; the move, the visa, the illness or the caring work was, and the plan is still a plan.
That the person has simply not found anybody.
Saying what the real constraint is, so that help is aimed at the constraint and not at the wrong problem.

sections.body:
None of this is a treatment, and none of it is a programme for a better life. It is maintenance: five habits that keep an ordinary life from becoming a fragile one. They are not glamorous, they are not specific to being single, and they work.

The order matters less than the doing. The first two build the structure that holds a week up. The third is the one most people put off. The last two are about keeping a door open without standing in the doorway.
examples: I keep Tuesday evenings for the people who live nearby.
I am not good at this, so I am going to ask you rather than manage it alone.
I am happy to meet people, but I am not going to turn every evening into an audition.
One hour a day with no screen and nobody in it.
sections.heading: How to live a single life well
steps: Build a routine that does not depend on anybody else. Fix the hour you wake, the days you work, the evening you exercise, the evening you call somebody. In a single life nobody else holds the shape of the week, so the shape has to come from somewhere.

Keep the friendships alive on purpose. Do not wait for a reason. A message with nothing in it — a photograph of the weather, a bad joke about the meeting — keeps the channel open, and a channel that is open is the one you can use when something goes wrong.

Ask for help earlier than feels reasonable. A person who has been single for years is usually good at handling things alone, and that skill is exactly what makes asking difficult. The practice is small: name the thing you cannot do, name the person who can, and ask.

Stay open without forcing. There is a difference between being available and being available to everybody. Keep the door open to people you actually like, and keep the rest of the week free of the pressure to meet somebody.
Protect the time alone. Rest needs an hour with nobody in it. Put the notifications away, do not fill the quiet with noise, and let some evenings be empty on purpose.

sections.body:
Read this if you are single now, and read it if you are single again after years of being with somebody. Read it if you are the one who asks the questions, and if you are the one who answers them. It is a vocabulary, not a remedy.

Nothing here says that a long single life is the better life, and nothing here says it is the worse one. People argue about that, and the argument is not settled. What this article does is give the reader the words for the situation and the practical steps that tend to help, so that a conversation about it can be had without guessing.

And nothing here is a plan for fixing anybody. If somebody is unhappy, the first question is not how to get them a partner. It is what in their life is actually the problem: the work, the money, the health, the house, the friendship, the hours. A person can be single and doing well. A person can be partnered and doing badly. The label starts the conversation; it does not finish it.
examples: This is a vocabulary, not a remedy.
Being single is not a diagnosis, and it is not a defect.
I am not going to tell you what to do with your life. I am giving you the words for it.
sections.heading: This article is not a programme

sections.body:
These are the sentences the reader will need most often, in the four situations that come up again and again: a colleague who asks, a relative who asks and adds an opinion, a first meeting where the question has to be answered once, and somebody who has already decided that you are lonely.

The first group keeps the answer short and moves on. The second group is for family, where the question arrives with a view attached. The third group is for a new room, where the point is to be understood once and then never to be asked again. The fourth group is for correcting a mistake in somebody's head, without turning it into a fight.
examples: I am single, but I am fine — how was your week?
Nobody at the moment. I am enjoying the quiet, actually.
I have got plans for the weekend, thanks for asking.
There is nobody in particular, and I am not in a hurry.
You do not need to worry about me. I am not lonely.
When I meet somebody, you will be the first to know.
Single at the moment, and not looking for anything in particular. It is good to meet you.
I live on my own and I like it. What do you do outside work?
I spend most of my weekends with friends and in the gym.
Being single is not the same as being lonely, and I am not lonely.
I know you mean well, but there is nothing here that needs fixing.
You are right that it is unusual. I am still fine with it.
sections.heading: Sentences you can use

item.summary: Long-term singleness has a vocabulary of its own, and much of the trouble around it comes from using the wrong word. After reading this you can tell the state of being single from the story a person tells about it, name the words that describe it precisely, recognise the pressure underneath it, and answer the questions other people ask without apologising for the answer.
item.title: The Psychology of Long-Term Singleness
